name: Losoong and the Kagyed dances in Gangtok
when: December, at the end of the harvest (Tibetan lunar calendar)
summary: Losoong is the Bhutia harvest festival and Sikkimese new year, called Namsoong by the Lepchas. In Gangtok it is preceded by the Kagyed masked dances at the Tsuklakhang royal chapel, with more cham at Rumtek and Phodong, archery and the burning of effigies.
body: Losoong marks the end of the farming year, when the harvest is in and households prepare for the new one. It grew out of the same roots as Losar, the Tibetan new year, and in Sikkim it belongs above all to the Bhutia community; Lepcha families keep it as Namsoong. Celebrations begin with offerings of chi, the local fermented millet drink, to the protective deities, and include the burning of an effigy of the demon king, which stands for clearing away the evil of the old year.

For visitors the most public part comes just before, with the Kagyed cham at Tsuklakhang, the royal chapel of the old Chogyals in Gangtok. Monks in masks and brocade dance episodes linked to Guru Padmasambhava, and at the end effigies and offerings are burnt. Masked dances are also held at Rumtek and at Phodong in North Sikkim, so a December trip can take in two monasteries.

Losoong is also a social time: archery contests, family feasts with meat, rice and home brew, and visits between villages. Dates follow the lunar calendar, so they move by a few weeks each year. December is cold but usually clear, which also makes it a good month for Kanchenjunga views. Check current status and dates before you travel.
tips: Ask your hotel or the Sikkim Tourism office in Gangtok for the year's Kagyed date, then plan around it, since the lunar date shifts.
Reach Tsuklakhang early; the palace courtyard is small and the best standing room fills well before the dancing starts.
Do not use flash or walk across the dance ground, and ask before photographing monks or families at close range.

faqs.q: When is Losoong celebrated in Sikkim?
faqs.a: Losoong falls in December, at the end of the harvest season, on a date set by the Tibetan lunar calendar, so it moves by a few weeks from year to year. The Kagyed masked dances at Tsuklakhang in Gangtok come a few days before. Check the current year's dates with Sikkim Tourism or your hotel before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Losoong and Losar?
faqs.a: Losoong is the Sikkimese Bhutia harvest festival and new year, held in December; Lepchas call it Namsoong. Losar is the Tibetan new year, held in February or March. Losoong was adapted from Losar traditions, which is why both include cham dances and offerings, but they are separate festivals about two months apart.

faqs.q: Where can we see the masked dances before Losoong?
faqs.a: In Gangtok, the Kagyed cham is held at Tsuklakhang, the royal chapel near the old palace. Masked dances are also performed at Rumtek, about an hour from Gangtok, and at Phodong in North Sikkim. Entry is generally free for spectators, but space is limited, so arrive early and dress warmly.

faqs.q: Is December a good time to visit Gangtok for Losoong?
faqs.a: Yes, if you pack for the cold. Gangtok nights drop to about 4–5 °C, skies are usually clear, and Kanchenjunga shows well in the mornings. Tsomgo Lake may be partly frozen and the Nathu La road can close after snowfall, so keep a spare day. Check current status before you travel.

name: Pang Lhabsol at Tsuklakhang
when: Aug–Sep, 15th day of the 7th Tibetan month
summary: Pang Lhabsol is Sikkim's own festival, held for Mount Kanchenjunga as the guardian deity of the land. It recalls the blood-brotherhood pact between the Lepcha and Bhutia peoples, and its warrior dances at the Tsuklakhang royal chapel in Gangtok are found nowhere else.
body: Most Buddhist festivals in these hills are shared with Tibet or Bhutan. Pang Lhabsol belongs to Sikkim. It honours Kanchenjunga, Dzo-nga to the Sikkimese, as the protective deity of the country, along with Yabdu, the mountain's commander. The festival is credited to the third Chogyal, Chakdor Namgyal, who reigned in the late 17th and early 18th centuries.

It also remembers an older event. Sikkimese tradition tells of a pact sworn at Kabi Lungchok in North Sikkim between the Lepcha chief Thekong Tek and the Bhutia ancestor Khye Bumsa, with the mountain gods as witnesses: the two peoples would be brothers. Pang Lhabsol keeps that story alive as a festival of unity between Sikkim's communities.

In Gangtok, the centre of the festival is the Tsuklakhang royal chapel, where monks perform the Pangtoed cham, a warrior dance in which dancers in helmets and armour, carrying swords and shields, represent Kanchenjunga and its retinue. It falls in the late monsoon, so carry rain gear and expect wet roads to the high passes. Check current status and dates before you travel.
tips: Combine Pang Lhabsol with a quiet late-monsoon stay: Gangtok hotels are cheaper in August and September than in October.
Arrive at Tsuklakhang early and stand where the stewards ask; the courtyard is small and the dancers need the full ground.
Keep a flexible day for Tsomgo, since late-monsoon landslides can close the road for hours.

faqs.a: Pang Lhabsol is a Sikkimese festival honouring Mount Kanchenjunga as the guardian deity of Sikkim. It is credited to the third Chogyal, Chakdor Namgyal, and recalls the blood-brotherhood pact between the Lepcha chief Thekong Tek and Khye Bumsa, ancestor of the Bhutia rulers. Its highlight is the warrior cham at Tsuklakhang in Gangtok.

It falls on the 15th day of the seventh month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, which lands in late August or September. The exact date changes every year, so confirm with Sikkim Tourism or your hotel. Check current status before you travel, as late-monsoon weather can also affect road travel to Gangtok.

faqs.q: Where is the best place to watch Pang Lhabsol?
faqs.a: The Tsuklakhang royal chapel in Gangtok holds the best-known celebration, with the Pangtoed warrior dance in the palace courtyard. Ravangla in South Sikkim also holds a large celebration. In Gangtok, come early, as space around the courtyard is limited and the best positions fill quickly.

faqs.q: Is the monsoon a problem for visiting during Pang Lhabsol?
faqs.a: It can be. Pang Lhabsol falls at the tail of the monsoon, so expect rain, slippery lanes and possible landslides on NH10, which has had repeated closures since the October 2023 Teesta flood. Build in a buffer day each way, carry a rain jacket and check current status before you travel.

name: Saga Dawa procession in Gangtok
when: May–Jun, full moon of the 4th Tibetan month
summary: Saga Dawa marks the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and passing into parinirvana. In Gangtok, monks and lay people carry the holy scriptures in a procession through town, with horns, drums and butter lamps, on the full moon of the fourth Tibetan month.
body: The fourth month of the Tibetan calendar, Saga Dawa, is the holiest of the year for Tibetan Buddhists, and its full moon is held to be the day of the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and parinirvana. Good deeds and prayers made in this month are believed to be multiplied many times, so monasteries are busy and many families give alms or free captive animals.

In Gangtok, the day is marked by a procession. Monks in maroon robes, playing long horns, cymbals and drums, walk through the town with lay devotees carrying the scriptures wrapped in cloth on their shoulders. The procession passes through the main roads of the capital, and shops and offices along the route pause to watch. Monasteries hold prayers and butter lamp offerings through the day.

Saga Dawa falls in late May or June, at the start of the monsoon, so mornings may be clear and afternoons wet. It is a respectful, quiet event rather than a show; stand back from the route, do not cut through the line and follow local people's lead. The date changes each year with the moon; check current status before you travel.
tips: Ask your hotel where the procession will pass this year, and find a spot on the route by mid-morning.
Many devotees avoid meat on the day, so vegetarian food is easier to find than usual in Buddhist homes and eateries.
Pack a rain layer: Saga Dawa often coincides with the first heavy monsoon showers.

faqs.a: Saga Dawa is the holiest month of the Tibetan Buddhist year. Its full moon, Saga Dawa Duchen, commemorates the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and parinirvana. In Sikkim it is a public holiday, and Gangtok marks it with a procession carrying the Buddhist scriptures through town, alongside prayers and butter lamp offerings at the monasteries.

faqs.q: When is Saga Dawa in Gangtok?
faqs.a: It falls on the full moon of the fourth Tibetan month, usually in late May or June. The exact date changes every year with the lunar calendar. Check the current year's date with Sikkim Tourism or your hotel, and check current status before you travel, since the monsoon may be starting.

faqs.q: Can tourists join the Saga Dawa procession?
faqs.a: Visitors can watch respectfully from the roadside, and nobody will mind quiet photography from a distance. Do not walk through the procession line, do not use flash on the scriptures or monks, and follow the lead of local people. Many visitors also spin prayer wheels at Do-drul Chorten, which is busy all day.

faqs.q: What else is good to do in Gangtok around Saga Dawa?
faqs.a: Late May and June are good for Tsomgo Lake after the snow thaw, the flower displays in Gangtok, and monastery visits at Rumtek and Enchey. Afternoons can be wet, so plan sightseeing for mornings. The Silk Route is still open but monsoon landslides begin in June; check current status before you travel.

name: Losar at Rumtek
summary: Losar, the Tibetan new year, is celebrated at Rumtek, the Karma Kagyu seat inaugurated on Losar 1966. In the days before, monks perform protector dances to clear the old year's obstacles; then families visit the monastery in their best clothes with offerings.
body: Rumtek has a special tie to Losar: the 16th Karmapa formally inaugurated the rebuilt monastery as the Dharma Chakra Centre on Losar in 1966. The new year is still the biggest occasion in its calendar. In the last days of the old year, the monks perform cham, masked protector dances meant to drive out the obstacles and negative forces of the year that is ending, followed by the burning of ritual offerings.

On Losar itself, the mood changes. Families from the villages around Rumtek and from Gangtok come in new clothes, bringing khadas (white scarves), butter and grain, and the courtyard fills with prayer, greetings and new prayer flags. Homes make khapse, fried pastries, and serve butter tea and chang. Visitors are welcome to watch quietly from the edges.

Losar falls in February or March and its date changes each year. Rumtek is about 24 km from Gangtok, so it works as a half-day or full-day trip, or stay nearby for an early start. Expect security checks at the gate and carry photo ID. Check current status and dates before you travel.
tips: Confirm the dance dates locally: the cham before Losar is the main visual event, and it is not on Losar day itself.
Leave Gangtok early or stay near Rumtek; shared taxis fill fast on festival mornings.
Bring a khada if you wish to make an offering, and keep to the edges of the courtyard during rituals.

faqs.q: When is Losar celebrated at Rumtek?
faqs.a: Losar, the Tibetan new year, falls in February or March on a date set by the lunar calendar. At Rumtek, the masked protector dances are held in the last days of the old year, just before Losar. Dates change annually, so confirm with the monastery office or your Gangtok hotel and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Why is Losar important at Rumtek?
faqs.a: Besides being the new year, Losar is the anniversary of Rumtek's rebirth: the 16th Karmapa inaugurated the rebuilt monastery as the Dharma Chakra Centre on Losar in 1966, after arriving from Tibet in 1959. The festival is the monastery's biggest occasion, drawing families from across East Sikkim.

faqs.q: How do we get to Rumtek from Gangtok for Losar?
faqs.a: Rumtek is about 24 km from Gangtok, roughly an hour by road. Shared taxis leave from Gangtok for about ₹80–150 a seat, but fill quickly on festival mornings, so go early. A reserved car costs roughly ₹1,500–2,500 for the return trip. Carry photo ID for the security check at the monastery gate.

faqs.q: Can visitors photograph the Losar dances at Rumtek?
faqs.a: Photography from the courtyard edges is usually allowed during outdoor dances, but rules can differ by day and inside prayer halls it is often not allowed. Never use flash, never step onto the dance ground and follow any instruction from monks or stewards. Ask before photographing families making offerings.
